title: Papirak the Strange
dek: Pristinia’s chaotic but extraordinary old wizard: once Papirus the Ardent, later a teacher of generations whose magic and unfinished work outlived him.

body:
Papirak the Strange was Pristinia’s erratic archmage, a guardian and teacher whose Training Dungeon prepared generations of adventurers. He could forget the people standing in his hut, lose the name of a spell, threaten someone for calling him old, and then demonstrate magic far beyond what his outward confusion suggested. His diminished reliability did not make his knowledge or power imaginary.

Pristinia buried him on 30 September 2026 beside the hill and Dungeon through which it knew him. His students, hidden grimoire, magical structures, and unfinished work continue to affect the living.

The person beneath the noise

Papirak was proud, impatient, impulsive, forgetful, unexpectedly generous, and often funny. After students helped him find a spell, he insisted that he had found it by himself. He could give away his hat while insulting the recipient’s hairline, stuff clues into his pockets, or casually alter a drink into a local “Papirak special.” The confusion was real; so was the desire to help.

His quieter moments prevent the comedy from becoming his whole biography. Late in life he could sit alone in a rocking chair beside a small fire, losing thoughts about the day and his own history before he could hold them. He was a damaged person, not an omniscient teacher pretending to be foolish.

Papirus the Ardent

The younger wizard encountered during the Gate-era temporal event was Papirus the Ardent, the same person later known as Papirak. On 30 December 2024, St. Anky, Olokun, Cecil, Coralyn, and Fenwick witnessed ancient Prima while the Gate was being built. Olokun recognized Papirus, and the scene’s narration confirmed the identification.

The observed past lay roughly two thousand years earlier. A frightened worker called Papirus the greatest wizard alive and said he had promised to hide and protect civilians. That is an attributed contemporary reputation. His involvement in the Gate’s construction is established; sole authorship of the Gate is not. The source name is Ardent; “Argent” is not treated as an independently established title.

How he survived that span remains unknown. The record does not establish immortality, cloning, undeath, or another mechanism. The restricted history behind his later condition remains in the keeper record.

Training before danger

The Training Dungeon was an institution rather than a collection of disposable encounters. Its magic was read as at least eighth-circle, and Scribonia described a remarkable system of illusion and refinement. Papirak could structure dangerous lessons, control or dismiss creatures, and use projections and expanded magical spaces. During an early exercise he used Revivify to bring a fallen student back with an exuberant “Wakey Wakey!”

His teaching was badly delivered but frequently practical: encounter a danger before facing it outside, learn what a creature can do, test a theory, and record what survives the test. Correction in training did not make every real-world failure reversible.

See. Read books, find lost knowledge. Write it down.Papirak

When challenged about his ability, his response was pointed: “What spell do you think me dungeon is?” The scale of the work outlived the creator’s ability to explain it consistently.

A small hut and a huge maze

Papirak lived in a humble hut on his hill near Pristinia. His maze, ancient labyrinth, and hidden stores were far larger and more sophisticated than the house suggested. Hearing that adventurers had lost powerful items reminded him of treasures he had hidden and wanted them to recover, although he could no longer reliably recall where he had put them.

Investigators inferred that he had once hidden the cache intelligently inside the mountain. His explanation that a shadowy demon made him forget remains his damaged recollection, not a confirmed cause. The labyrinth’s resemblance to the Training Dungeon and the drawings in his pockets supplied clues without settling every mystery.

Extraordinary power, uncertain reliability

Advanced illusion, concealment, warding, magical spaces, hidden writing, creature control, and resurrection in training are part of his recovered capabilities. He threatened Disintegrate when called old and once searched for Suffocate because a deer was eating his broccoli. A threat is not proof that every threatened spell was cast.

No definitive level, challenge rating, hit-point total, or complete spell list is established. His arcane capability and his cognitive reliability are different parts of the record.

The loss of a teacher and witness

Magnus attacked Papirak while seeking knowledge locked in his mind, and Papirak died afterward. Later characters, including Scribonia, attribute his death to Magnus. That attribution preserves the assault’s causal responsibility; the exact restricted sequence belongs in the keeper account.

His death removed a living witness to ancient history as well as a teacher. Later discoveries must come through surviving artifacts, records, memories, and other witnesses rather than assuming that his missing knowledge can simply be reconstructed.

The people who carried him forward

  • Scribonia survived his training, mourned his failure to protect him, and promised to study the Dungeon and leave part of himself in Pristinia to guard, teach, and aid. The promise is established; complete restoration is not.
  • Melian Starguard remembered the strange, lost light that remained his own and led the town’s funeral rite.
  • Fenwick d’Jorasco witnessed Papirus in the ancient temporal event, later noticed the absent spellbook, and protected the staff for burial instead of claiming it.
  • Pappy bantered with Papirak and poured whiskey at his funeral. His story of completing the Gate together remains an attributed funeral claim.
  • Pell prepared the body, arranged the mausoleum, and completed the practical work of burial.
  • Carmen was someone he called “my dearest Carmen.” The full nature and history of the relationship remain unresolved.

An inheritance distributed through Pristinia

The town’s funeral honored the wizard it had actually known: the teacher who shouted, forgot names, revived students, and tried to make them harder to kill. His walking stick was revealed as a Staff of Power, made from a cherry tree planted on his wedding day and given by his wife. Melian’s public decision left it with him; Fenwick’s Sequester explains why it later escaped magical detection.

His grimoire had already left his custody before his death. Its later hidden spells did not begin to exist when someone finally saw them. The legacy record preserves the custody chain and funeral, while the mausoleum records his protected resting place. His work has no single established heir.

The open record

His longevity, exact technical role in creating the Gate, complete grimoire, remaining caches, and the scope of what can be recovered from the Dungeon remain unresolved. The dates of his final attack and death are not supplied here as newly established facts. Scribonia’s confidence in restoration does not prove a complete recovery will occur.
